{{short description|Infinite series of Bessel functions}}
{{Improve categories|date=August 2025}}In [[mathematics]], '''Fourier–Bessel series''' is a particular kind of [[generalized Fourier series]] (an [[infinite series]] expansion on a finite interval) based on [[Bessel function]]s.

Fourier–Bessel series are used in the solution to [[partial differential equation]]s, particularly in [[cylindrical coordinate]] systems.

== Definition ==

The Fourier–Bessel series of a function {{math|''f''(''x'')}} with a [[Domain of a function|domain]] of {{closed-closed|0, ''b''}} satisfying {{math|1=''f''(''b'') = 0}}
[[File:Basisweki.jpg|thumb|361x361px|Bessel function for (i) <math>\alpha=0</math> and (ii) <math>\alpha=1</math>.]]
<math display="block">f: [0,b] \to \R</math>
is the representation of that function as a [[linear combination]] of many [[orthogonal]] versions of the same [[Bessel functions of the first kind|Bessel function of the first kind]] ''J''<sub>''α''</sub>, where the argument to each version ''n'' is differently scaled, according to <ref>{{Cite book |last1=Magnus |first1=Wilhelm |last2=Oberhettinger |first2=Fritz |last3=Soni |first3=Raj Pal |date=1966 |title=Formulas and Theorems for the Special Functions of Mathematical Physics |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-11761-3 |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-11761-3|isbn=978-3-662-11763-7 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=R. |first=Smythe, William |title=Static and dynamic electricity. - 3rd ed. |date=1968 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |oclc=878854927}}</ref>
<math display="block">(J_\alpha )_n (x) := J_\alpha \left( \frac{u_{\alpha,n}}b x \right)</math>
where ''u''<sub>''α'',''n''</sub> is a [[Root of a function|root]], numbered ''n'' associated with the Bessel function ''J''<sub>''α''</sub> and ''c''<sub>''n''</sub> are the assigned coefficients:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schroeder |first=Jim |date=April 1993 |title=Signal Processing via Fourier-Bessel Series Expansion |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1006/dspr.1993.1016 |journal=Digital Signal Processing |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=112–124 |doi=10.1006/dspr.1993.1016 |bibcode=1993DSP.....3..112S |issn=1051-2004|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
<math display="block">f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n J_\alpha \left( \frac{u_{\alpha,n}}b x \right). </math>

== Interpretation ==

The Fourier–Bessel series may be thought of as a Fourier expansion in the ρ coordinate of [[cylindrical coordinates]]. Just as the [[Fourier series]] is defined for a finite interval and has a counterpart, the [[continuous Fourier transform]] over an infinite interval, so the Fourier–Bessel series has a counterpart over an infinite interval, namely the [[Hankel transform]].

== Calculating the coefficients ==

As said, differently scaled Bessel Functions are orthogonal with respect to the [[inner product]]
[[File:Fbsecofspeech.jpg|thumb|341x341px|(i) Speech signal (mtlb.mat from Matlab toolbox), (ii) FBSE coefficients of speech signal, and (iii) magnitude of FBSE coefficients of speech signal.]]
<math display="block">\langle f,g \rangle = \int_0^b  x f(x) g(x) \, dx</math>

according to

<math display="block">\int_0^b x J_\alpha\left(\frac{x u_{\alpha,n}}{b}\right)\,J_\alpha\left(\frac{x u_{\alpha,m}}{b}\right)\,dx
= \frac{b^2}{2} \delta_{mn}[J_{\alpha+1}(u_{\alpha,n})]^2,</math>

(where: <math>\delta_{mn}</math> is the Kronecker delta). The coefficients can be obtained from [[Vector projection|projecting]] the function {{math|''f''(''x'')}} onto the respective Bessel functions:

<math display="block">c_n = \frac{ \langle f,(J_\alpha)_n \rangle }{ \langle (J_\alpha)_n,(J_\alpha)_n \rangle } = \frac{ \int_0^b  x f(x) (J_\alpha)_n(x) \, dx }{ \frac12 (b J_{\alpha\pm1}(u_{\alpha,n}))^2}</math>

where the plus or minus sign is equally valid.

For the inverse transform, one makes use of the following representation of the [[Dirac delta function]]<ref name="Cahill">{{cite book |last1=Cahill |first1=Kevin |title=Physical Mathematics |date=2019 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9781108470032 |pages=385 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/physical-mathematics/060AA74620B6D8574DE841A8836D1D35 |access-date=9 March 2023}}</ref>

<math display="block">\frac{2 x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}}{b^2} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{J_\alpha\left(\frac{x u_{\alpha,k}}{b}\right)\,J_\alpha\left(\frac{y u_{\alpha,k}}{b}\right)}{J_{\alpha+1}^2(u_{\alpha,k})}
= \delta(x-y).</math>

== Applications ==

The Fourier–Bessel series expansion employs aperiodic and decaying Bessel functions as the basis. The Fourier–Bessel series expansion has been successfully applied in diversified areas such as Gear fault diagnosis,<ref>{{Citation |last1=D’Elia |first1=Gianluca |chapter=On the Use of Fourier-Bessel Series Expansion for Gear Diagnostics |date=2012 |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-28768-8_28 |title=Condition Monitoring of Machinery in Non-Stationary Operations |pages=267–275 |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-642-28767-1 |access-date=2022-10-22 |last2=Delvecchio |first2=Simone |last3=Dalpiaz |first3=Giorgio|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-28768-8_28 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> discrimination of odorants in a turbulent ambient,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Vergaraa |first1=A. |last2=Martinelli |first2=E. |last3=Huerta |first3=R. |last4=D’Amico |first4=A. |last5=Di Natale |first5=C. |date=2011 |title=Orthogonal Decomposition of Chemo-Sensory Signals: Discriminating Odorants in a Turbulent Ambient |journal=Procedia Engineering |volume=25 |pages=491–494 |doi=10.1016/j.proeng.2011.12.122 |issn=1877-7058|doi-access=free }}</ref> postural stability analysis, detection of voice onset time, glottal closure instants (epoch) detection, separation of speech formants, speech enhancement,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gurgen |first1=F.S. |last2=Chen |first2=C.S. |date=1990 |title=Speech enhancement by fourier–bessel coefficients of speech and noise |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1049/ip-i-2.1990.0040 |journal=IEE Proceedings I - Communications, Speech and Vision |volume=137 |issue=5 |pages=290 |doi=10.1049/ip-i-2.1990.0040 |issn=0956-3776|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and speaker identification.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gopalan |first1=K. |last2=Anderson |first2=T.R. |last3=Cupples |first3=E.J. |date=May 1999 |title=A comparison of speaker identification results using features based on cepstrum and Fourier-Bessel expansion |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1109/89.759036 |journal=IEEE Transactions on Speech and Audio Processing |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=289–294 |doi=10.1109/89.759036 |issn=1063-6676|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Fourier–Bessel series expansion has also been used to reduce cross terms in the Wigner–Ville distribution.

==Dini series==

A second Fourier–Bessel series, also known as ''Dini series'', is associated with the [[Robin boundary condition]]
<math display="block">b f'(b) + c f(b) = 0 ,</math> where <math>c</math> is an arbitrary constant.
The Dini series can be defined by
<math display="block">f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n J_\alpha(\gamma_n x/b),</math>

where <math>\gamma_n</math> is the ''n''-th zero of <math>x J'_\alpha(x) + c J_\alpha(x)</math>.

The coefficients <math>b_n</math> are given by
<math display="block">
b_n = \frac{2 \gamma_n^2}{ b^2(c^2+\gamma_n^2-\alpha^2)J_\alpha^2(\gamma_n)} 
\int_0^b J_\alpha(\gamma_n x/b)\,f(x) \,x \,dx.
</math>
